episode_title: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us

stories.summary: Cavalli-Sforza, a scientist born around 1918, was obsessed with the deep past at a time when the only tools were fossils, ruins and early carbon dating. Scant data from these sources had hardened into conventional wisdom. He first tried reading history through the blood groups of different populations. In the early 1960s he made a bet that seemed insane: human history would be revealed through our genes. The human genome wasn't fully sequenced until 2001. Mitochondrial DNA work in the 1980s showed we all came out of Africa. By around 2009, full-genome studies of the past were a mature science, and his vision had come true.
stories.insight: Visionary science often commits to a kind of evidence decades before the technology exists to collect it. When that evidence finally arrives, it can overturn a century of confident consensus.
stories.quote: And his bet was that we shall find out about human history, about humanity, about how we came to be, through genetic trails

stories.summary: Drawing on Tony Joseph's Early Indians, Amit traces four major migrations into the subcontinent. The 'first Indians' came out of Africa about 65,000 years ago; tribal communities carry more of their genes today. Agricultural people from Central Asia came next, brought wheat and barley, and formed the Harappan civilisation. They probably spoke a proto-Dravidian language, an early form of Tamil, which is older than Sanskrit. Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman peoples arrived in the north-east. Around 2000 BCE came Indo-European speakers from the steppes, carrying an early form of Sanskrit. Their descendants mixed into 'Ancient North Indians' and 'Ancient South Indians', and every Indian carries both in differing degrees.
stories.insight: The genetic data rules out both politically convenient myths. There was no clean Aryan invasion, and Aryans were not the original people from whom everything came. What happened was migration followed by deep mixing.
stories.quote: What really happened the way modern scientists would like to talk of it is that there was an Aryan migration. Right, it wasn't an invasion

stories.summary: From Peggy Mohan's Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: Sanskrit is not a pure Indo-European language. It has retroflex sounds, made with the tongue curled up toward the roof of the mouth. Amit demonstrates these with Hindi word pairs. Persian and other Indo-European neighbours to the west lack these sounds, but the Dravidian languages the migrants met in India have them. The mechanism was intimate. The migrants were mostly men who married local women. Children spent their early years speaking their mother's tongue, and boys later learned the men's language through apprenticeship and hunting. Vedic Sanskrit emerged as a blend, was later frozen as a language of learning for a class and caste, and became a dead language like Latin. Prakrit kept evolving.
stories.insight: Even a 'sacred' classical language is a hybrid. Languages carry the imprint of who raised the children, not just who held power.
stories.quote: Sanskrit, even if it came out of the Indo European languages, is not a pure Indo European language.

stories.topic: When the Great Party Ended: Caste Endogamy Around 100 CE
stories.summary: For roughly two thousand years after the Indo-Europeans arrived, the genetic evidence shows full intermingling. Nobody was drawing lines between 'our people' and 'not our people'. Around 100 CE a particular ideological strand in the Gangetic belt won out, and severe caste endogamy began. It left a clear signature in the genes. Upper-caste men also proved more successful at spreading their genes than lower-caste men.
stories.insight: Caste endogamy is real and visible in our DNA, but it is about two thousand years old, while the mixing is about four thousand. It was a path India took, not a destiny, and it can be reversed.
stories.quote: if you're looking for a large population, look at the Han Chinese, they're a large population. India is many thousands of small populations.

stories.summary: About 25 years ago Amit had a Standard Chartered credit card with no auto-pay. Being, as he puts it, a lazy Bengali, he relied on the bank calling him so he could send someone to collect payment. Once the outstanding was so small, Rs 80, that nobody called. The card was cancelled and his CIBIL score collapsed. With interest the amount grew to Rs 3,000, then Rs 5,000, then Rs 29,000. The bank refused to send a bill and abusive recovery agents made threats. He refused on principle to pay, even though he easily could have. His score is still bad today. He pays vendors immediately or even in advance, and has never had an EMI.
stories.insight: A single traditional metric can badly misjudge a person. Richer behavioural data could build a far more holistic, and fairer, picture of who someone really is.
stories.quote: And yet I fancy that if you could see all the other data about me, you would realize that I'm an absolutely upstanding citizen.

stories.topic: Your Phone Battery as a Credit Score
stories.summary: Smart Finance, a Chinese micro-lender, scores borrowers from their phone data. If your battery regularly falls below 12%, you won't get a loan. So will filling in your birth date too fast, or making a typo and going back to fix it. Lenddo found the opposite extreme also bad: a phone that is always fully charged signals an unreliable borrower, so there is a sweet spot. Amit keeps his phone around 80%. Tala, which operates in Africa and Asia, penalises frequent small recharges and looks at how many of your contacts have repaid loans. A 2018 German study found iPhone users default less than Android users (roughly 1.07% vs 1.7%). It also found that Hotmail or Yahoo addresses, typos in your email, and habitual 2 AM shopping predict higher default.
stories.insight: Nobody starts with a theory that low battery means risk. The algorithm finds the pattern across millions of phones, and the 'why' is left for humans to work out. That makes the system hard to game.
stories.quote: if your battery on your phone goes below twelve percent regularly, they will not give you a loan.

stories.summary: After COVID struck, researchers in India and elsewhere used phone location data. It showed the lockdown largely worked, with the migrant-labour exodus as the exception. It also showed that recovery did not begin when the government said it was safe; people stayed wary for a while. The data could flag likely surges when festivals like Diwali drew crowds, which markets could use to predict demand for drugs or masks. Ajay adds that Google and Facebook released mobility measures for the whole country.
stories.insight: What people actually do, captured passively, can diverge sharply from official declarations. Public release of such data is a public good.
stories.quote: it was just like a gorgeous public domain data release that they did that helped everybody to understand the pandemic better.

stories.topic: The Diamond Brothers and the Walmart Parking Lot
stories.summary: In 2009 Tom Diamond visited his brother Alex, who worked at a satellite-imagery firm. Alex had just used imagery to confirm that a factory a client wanted to buy was representing itself honestly. While the brothers were jamming (their hobby was rock versions of Western classical music, including Schubert), they remembered Sam Walton's habit. The Walmart founder judged how a store was doing by counting cars in its parking lot. Why not do that for every store? Alex quit, bought three years of imagery and back-tested it. Parking-lot traffic predicted quarterly results. They founded RS Metrics (RS for remote sensing), and UBS came calling. Ajay's nephew joined later. Early on they got only about twelve expensive pictures a month; the data later became cheap and plentiful, birthing the 'alt data' industry. For Tesla production they once flew their own plane overhead. Two Berkeley professors later used parking data from 67,000 stores and estimated a 4.7% edge over ordinary investors, when traders would die for 0.2%.
stories.insight: An old shopkeeper's intuition plus new measurement became an industry. Satellite pictures of parking lots are really pictures of real people buying real things.
stories.quote: Sam Walton, who founded Walmart, once said that he would get a sense of how well the business is doing by seeing how many cars are parked in the parking lot outside that particular Walmart he was looking at

stories.summary: A train carrying around 268 wagons of iron ore crashed and capsized. Stock prices fell, iron ore prices rose, and the market priced in the expected loss. Traders who checked satellite images saw the ore was just lying flat and easy to reload. They bet the market would recover faster than expected and made a killing.
stories.insight: Markets react to headlines. Whoever looks directly at reality, rather than reasoning from the news, holds the edge.
stories.quote: But there were smart people who looked at satellite data and they found that the iron ore was actually just lying flat and it would be easy to reload it again.

stories.topic: Reading Oil Tanks From Their Shadows
stories.summary: Many oil storage tanks have a roof that floats on the oil, so it sinks as the tank empties. The sun's position is known. When a tank is full there is no shadow inside it. As it empties, the sunken roof shows a shadow in an overhead satellite image, and the shadow's size tells you how full the tank is.
stories.insight: Simple geometry plus a camera in the sky can reveal private inventories. This is the kind of creative measurement that is reshaping what we can know.
stories.quote: when the tank is completely full, there's no shadow. When the tank falls, you start seeing the shadow of the sun in the vertical view of the satellite.

stories.topic: The Lipstick Index and Its COVID Exception
stories.summary: Amit quizzes Ajay, who guesses right: lipstick sales rise in tough times. Leonard Lauder of Estée Lauder coined the 'lipstick index' after sales rose during the 2001 recession. His logic was that people cut back on $200 handbags but still want to feel good, so they buy the cheapest luxury available, a $20 lipstick. The pattern held in 2008 and in 2011. COVID broke it, because masks made lipstick pointless.
stories.insight: Counterintuitive signals hide in everyday spending. Every index also rests on hidden assumptions, here that your face is seen, and it fails when those assumptions break.
stories.quote: in tough times people will stop buying two hundred dollars handbag, but they want to feel good about themselves, so they'll still buy twenty dollar lipsticks.

stories.topic: The Billion Prices Project Catches Argentina
stories.summary: Roberto Rigobon and Alberto Cavallo argued that economies are measured with too little data when far more is available online. So they scraped huge volumes of internet prices to build their own index. They found online prices track offline prices closely. For Argentina between 2007 and 2015, official inflation was about 7-10%, but their data showed 20-30% a year, and the crisis eventually exploded. Ajay has met Rigobon at conferences, knows his work on identification through heteroskedasticity, and says his own team intuitively reinvented part of that idea.
stories.insight: Independent, large-scale data can expose official statistics that understate the truth. The more diverse the sources behind an index, the more you can trust it.
stories.quote: If you're building an index, the more diverse sources you use, the better it is, the more reliable it is.

recommendations.item: Who We Are and How We Got Here: Ancient DNA and the new science of the human past
recommendations.creator: David Reich
recommendations.context: Named as one of 'two books that everyone should read' while introducing the genetics of prehistory.
recommendations.reason: Explains the science of full-genome studies and how they overturned received wisdom from archaeology. Amit says he hasn't stopped thinking about its findings since reading it years ago.

recommendations.item: Early Indians: The Story of Our Ancestors and Where We Came From
recommendations.creator: Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: The second of the 'two books that everyone should read', and the basis for Amit's account of India's four migrations.
recommendations.reason: Applies the genetic evidence to India: first Indians, Harappans, Ancient North and South Indians, and the Aryan migration. Amit calls its findings 'just stunning'.

recommendations.item: Tony Joseph on The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions his episode with Tony Joseph while recommending Early Indians.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation with the author about the same findings.

recommendations.item: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: The Story of India through Its Languages
recommendations.creator: Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: Called 'another great book' during the discussion of Sanskrit and the Aryan migration.
recommendations.reason: Does with language what Reich and Joseph did with genes. It is the source of the retroflex-sound and mothers'-tongue insights that 'blew my mind'.

recommendations.item: Peggy Mohan on The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside her book.
recommendations.reason: A long-form conversation with the author whose linguistic detective work underpins the Sanskrit discussion.

recommendations.item: A History of Hinduism (Ep 76 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while explaining how caste and religion followed different paths.
recommendations.reason: Their earlier episode built on Manu Pillai's account of Hinduism as an assimilative, almost 'open source' tradition.

recommendations.item: Gods, Guns and Missionaries: The Making of the Modern Hindu Identity
recommendations.creator: Manu Pillai
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'excellent', especially its introductory chapter on the history of Hinduism.
recommendations.reason: Shows how fluid Hinduism was for centuries, with Vaishnavites, Shaivites, sects and local customs all absorbed. That fluidity contrasts sharply with the rigidity of caste.

recommendations.creator: Ghazala Wahab
recommendations.context: Discussed on a recent Seen and the Unseen episode; cited in the census and categorisation discussion.
recommendations.reason: Has a 'great excerpt' on tribals made to tick a 'Hindu' box, and the mass movement now reasserting their earlier identities.

recommendations.item: Caste and the Census (Ep 417 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the context of debates over a caste census.
recommendations.reason: For anyone wanting the deeper debate on what counting caste could do to society.

recommendations.creator: George Soros
recommendations.context: Where Amit first learned the idea of reflexivity, which he applies to caste.
recommendations.reason: Source of the concept that the narratives imposed on a system change how that system sees and shapes itself.

recommendations.item: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Ep 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Recalled while arguing that markets and the 1991 reforms lifted hundreds of millions of Dalits.
recommendations.reason: The Dalit activist explains why his two heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith.

recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Amit had just finished it while discussing how homogenisation destroyed diversity.
recommendations.reason: Covers the diversity that existed before the agricultural age. He has some misgivings, but says parts are a masterpiece and promises to discuss it in detail later.

recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Recommended to the 'gentle reader' as Scott's earlier book.
recommendations.reason: To see the havoc the agricultural age brought to humankind. Amit's broader advice: 'you should read everything by James C Scott.'

recommendations.creator: Vinay Singhal
recommendations.context: Amit's example of markets reviving diversity in language.
recommendations.reason: A 'Netflix for Bharat' streaming content in dialects like Haryanvi and Bhojpuri at Netflix prices, with about four lakh subscribers four years ago. Amit believes in the project and its founder, and even tried to invest.

recommendations.item: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (Ep 291 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's conversation with the Stage founder four years ago.
recommendations.reason: The story behind a market bet on India's dialects.

recommendations.creator: Tobias Berg, Valentin Burg, Ana Gombović & Manju Puri
recommendations.context: The 2018 German study Amit cites in the phone-data chapter.
recommendations.reason: Shows that digital footprints predict default: iPhone vs Android, email provider, typos in email addresses, and late-night shopping.

recommendations.item: The Nighttime Lights of Russia (Ep 116 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous episode, which Amit 'really enjoyed'.
recommendations.reason: Shows how satellite night-lights let Indian researchers see into the Russian economy in ways traditional statistics never could.

recommendations.item: Shedding light on the Russia-Ukraine War
recommendations.creator: Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Susan Thomas
recommendations.context: The paper behind the nighttime-lights episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'just wonderful', and praises the authors for making their data freely available for anyone to play with.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Ep 20 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while linking the hemline index to fertility.
recommendations.reason: Contains Ajay's 'very deep point' that fertility tracks a nation's mood: people have fewer children in bad or authoritarian times.

core_ideas.concept: Data First, Then Regularities, Then Theory
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's model of how knowledge grows: Kepler measured and found statistical regularities, and only then did Newton build theory. Without measurement, debate is just opinion. India badly under-measures itself, and institutions like the CSO and CMIE were long the only game in town.
core_ideas.quote: You always start at the data. If you don't have the data, you don't have anything. Then it's just conversation.

core_ideas.explanation: Over the last twenty years, new data sources have given us 'new eyes': ancient DNA, satellite night-lights, phone footprints, parking-lot imagery. These let us see things old statistical systems never could, and they can decisively settle debates that careful archaeology or opinion never resolved.
core_ideas.quote: We brought guns to a knife fight and we settled these questions.

core_ideas.explanation: Nineteenth-century medicine relied on bloodletting, had no germ theory, and killed people in hospitals, which is partly why quack remedies thrived. We assume today's knowledge is near-final, but two centuries from now people will see us as equally ignorant. Genetics has just overturned much of what archaeology confidently believed.
core_ideas.quote: Don't think that where we have reached is the pinnacle of knowledge.

core_ideas.explanation: The key finding of ancient DNA is that humans are far more mixed than once assumed. All of us descend from 'mitochondrial Eve' in Africa, then mixed endlessly: five major migrations into Europe, four into India, and 3-5% Neanderthal ancestry in many Europeans and Asians. Visible differences exist, but beneath them is one deeply interwoven people.
core_ideas.quote: they all get mixed up with each other and we are all fundamentally one people.

core_ideas.explanation: A language is more than a tool for communication; it carries values. Japanese and Korean favour terse minimalism, while Urdu, Punjabi and Bengali are exuberant and expressive. English sits in a utilitarian middle, which is why Tagore loses something in English. Different languages may encourage different kinds of thinking and feeling.
core_ideas.quote: I often say that you should not think of a language as just a means of communication. A language encodes much else within it

core_ideas.concept: Caste: The Deepest Sin, Not the Original Sin
core_ideas.explanation: Genetics proves caste endogamy is real, harmful and about two thousand years old, so no spin can erase it. That is the sad story: it runs deep, and markets and urbanisation help but are no magic bullet. Amit argues that the 1991 reforms lifted hundreds of millions of Dalits and that Manmohan Singh did more for them than any twentieth-century thinker, while still crediting Ambedkar. The happy story is that the mixing is twice as old, so caste was a path chosen, not a fate, and it can be reversed.
core_ideas.quote: I think it's the deepest sin of Hinduism, but it's not the original sin

core_ideas.explanation: If marriage must stay within the caste, female sexuality has to be policed: no affairs, no children outside the group, no falling in love. Amit argues this created a sexually repressive society. Today's prudishness comes partly from this and partly from imported Victorian morality.
core_ideas.quote: one of the natural consequences of caste endogamy is that you want to control female sexuality.

core_ideas.concept: Legibility and Reflexivity: Measuring Changes the Measured
core_ideas.explanation: Amit lays out the theory that British census-takers, guided by Brahmin informants, forced fluid identities into fixed boxes of caste and religion, and that the boxes then shaped how people saw themselves. He calls this reflexivity, a term from Soros, and notes that tribals made to tick 'Hindu' are now pushing back. He holds that both this theory and the genetic evidence of real caste endogamy contain truth. Ajay frames it in terms of Seeing Like a State: state legibility projects have unintended consequences, a kind of Heisenberg effect.
core_ideas.quote: the state tried to make caste legible and in the process it changed the caste system.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Derive the Ought From the Is
core_ideas.explanation: Reich and Joseph both stress that genetic differences must never justify racist thinking. Amit invokes G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy and Hume's is-ought problem: that something is natural doesn't make it right. Differences, including those between men and women, deserve celebration, not enshrinement as rules or hierarchies.
core_ideas.quote: I think differences are amazing. Differences should be celebrated. We are different in all kinds of directions. We are far more alike than we are different, but the differences are not a problem.

core_ideas.explanation: Agriculture narrowed diversity: of some 200,000 plant varieties, about twelve dominate our diet, and four animal species dominate the landscape. There are three chickens for every human, all industrially farmed. Dialects like Bhojpuri, Maithili and Haryanvi were swallowed by big languages. Yet markets work in two phases: first they chase scale and homogenise, then they empower niches, as Stage.in shows. Diversity can return.
core_ideas.quote: the first impulse of markets was you go for scale and you homogenize, but the second empowering effect of markets is that you empower individuals to find the long tail

core_ideas.concept: Endogamy's Hidden Health Cost (Ajay's Open Question)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay asks whether smaller jatis fall below a minimum viable population, so that endogamy degrades their gene pool. If so, the spread of modernity and intermarriage would bring a large public-health gain. He also notes from travels in Mauritius and Sri Lanka that coasts and islands show more genetic diversity because sailors and traders mixed there for millennia. He wonders whether India's coasts have been measured this way.
core_ideas.quote: are all jatis in India big enough to be larger than a minimum viable population, or does endogamy lead to a damage in the quality of the gene pool for smaller jatis?

core_ideas.concept: Black-Box Metrics Are Hard to Game
core_ideas.explanation: Machine-learning credit models find patterns across millions of users without caring why they hold, much as AlphaZero taught chess players that initiative mattered more than they thought. A known metric, like battery level, can be gamed. Thousands of opaque ones cannot, even by the lender itself. Unlike China's state social credit score, this is voluntary: you trade access to your phone for a loan.
core_ideas.quote: if we know metrics we can game metrics. But we don't even know what the metrics are.

core_ideas.explanation: Ordinary life (emailing, shopping, buying vada pav) throws off a trail of data that looks like trash. People are now opening that garbage bin and finding powerful information in it.
core_ideas.quote: as a side effect of our normal life and activities, there is this digital exhaust of information that you might otherwise consider to be just trash.

core_ideas.concept: Privacy's First Enemy Is the State
core_ideas.explanation: Private firms using personal data need privacy rules, but those problems are qualitatively easier. India has it upside down: the government has unlimited access to personal information while restricting private firms. Google can do you little harm; the state can coerce you.
core_ideas.quote: If there is a need for protection, it is against the state.

core_ideas.concept: Smart Speculators Make Prices a Public Good
core_ideas.explanation: Critics call alt-data edges unfair. Ajay replies that finance rewards smart people for producing information, and their trading builds efficient prices that help the whole economy run. Speculation is voluntary and meant to be hard. Those who don't want to compete should buy and hold index funds.
core_ideas.quote: we should never get into this investor protection when we are discussing speculator protection.

core_ideas.concept: Weigh Your Data When Updating Beliefs
core_ideas.explanation: Comparing several measures of the same thing reveals the strengths and limits of each. All measurement ultimately serves the updating of priors, and how far you move should depend on how good the data is.
core_ideas.quote: if you see a weak data measure and it diverges from your prior, then you will change your prior less. Whereas if you see a really good data measure and it leads you to some conclusions that are quite different from your prior, then you should be changing your mind more.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit recalls Ajay's point, from his PhD on fertility, that people have fewer children in bad or authoritarian times, and wonders whether hemlines reflect the same mood. Ajay invokes Hannah Arendt's line that authoritarians run out of people to oppress. He cautions that the measure needs high-quality birth data, a privilege of rich countries like South Korea and Japan. He also notes recent claims that China's population is smaller than official figures say.
core_ideas.quote: you want the good life, you want a good society, and then people will have more children. Whereas when the world is more messed up, people will have less children.

core_ideas.concept: Everyday Behaviour as an Economic Barometer
core_ideas.explanation: Quirky indexes read the economy from ordinary choices. Lipstick sales rise in downturns. Men delay buying underwear (Greenspan's index). Hemlines rose in the 1920s and 1960s and fell in the Depression and after the 1973 oil shock. Tie sales fall with layoffs, though that may also reflect work from home. Diaper sales fell while rash-ointment sales rose in 2008. A stripper index (2021-22) tracked fewer high-value customers. The hard part is attribution: knowing what is really driving a signal.
core_ideas.quote: the question to ponder on is one of attributability. That if a particular part of the economy is doing well, why is it doing well?

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay introduces 'the great Omit Varma' in Bengali style. Amit replies that to Ajay he's Amit, 'just as you are Ajay and not Ajoy. Two can play this game. Kindly control.'
Amit, after Ajay's ode to data: 'the road to knowledge begins with data, and I would say the road to knowledge ends in despair.'

On all 7.5 billion humans descending from mitochondrial Eve: 'Why are you laughing? This is a serious subject. But I suspect the lady would also laugh if she knew what she had wrought. All for a few moments of pleasure.'
On 3-5% Neanderthal DNA in Europeans and Asians: 'we were having a party with Neanderthals'. So calling someone a Neanderthal who 'won't understand art' is really an insult to part of ourselves.
Amit teases Ajay for constantly texting: the crew wonders what he's up to, 'and you always say while you blush, I am checking the weather. I'm not so sure about that.'
Amit blames his credit-card fiasco on being Bengali ('because I'm Bengali I'd be lazy'). He has a credit card again only because, 'and this is a typical Indian story, a friend of mine runs a bank.'
Before the 4.7% parking-lot statistic, Amit borrows clickbait style: 'you won't believe what happened next.'
On saying 'indexes' rather than the British 'indices': it's sexier, 'because we don't talk of the sises, we talk of the sexes.'
The lipstick index failed during COVID: 'People are wearing masks so they don't need lipstick. You understand what I'm saying? This is a profound point.'

Introducing Greenspan's male underwear index, Amit describes him as an economist who 'loved low interest rates'. In bad times the gap between underwear purchases gets, pun not intended, 'stretched', until the elastic is falling off completely.

An unnamed older friend who played chess across Europe and the Soviet Union in the 1980s turned his underwear inside out when it got dirty, so 'every underwear is effectively like two underwear'. He also once traded his corduroys for sex in Russia. Amit: 'I think I've revealed who it is.'

On the hemline index: after the 1973 oil shock maxi skirts came into vogue, 'see the result of bad economics', which Amit finds 'utterly shocking'. He also tells Ajay he is 'spiritually a child of the sixties'.
On the diaper rash index: 'You simply have to get your babies all the diapers they need, which is a sentence I never thought I'd say.'

The closing 'EIE shirts index' stands at five: Ajay scores 9.5 and black-clad Amit 0.5 ('Black is a state of mind'). When Ajay once asked why Turn Black doesn't make its kurtas in white, he suggested launching 'Turn White'. Asked whether Ajay looks sexy because of the shirt or himself: 'Of course it's a shirt.'
Kepler and Newton: Ajay's model of science as measurement, then statistical regularities (Kepler's laws), then theory (Newton).
Nineteenth-century bloodletting and the absence of germ theory, which Amit says is why quack treatments like homeopathy flourished: the alternatives weren't much better.
Wittgenstein, invoked by Amit for the idea that language limits how much of the world we can express.
Tagore, whose own translations from Bengali into English don't sound as good, because the two languages hold different values.
G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy and David Hume's is-ought problem, cited against turning human differences into hierarchies.
James C Scott's Seeing Like a State: Ajay quips its alternative title could be 'State Legibility Projects Have Unintended Consequences'. He also calls census-making a Heisenberg effect.
'A language is a dialect with an army', the old line Amit uses to explain why Bhojpuri, Maithili and Haryanvi were swallowed by Hindi.
Chandra Bhan Prasad naming his two heroes as Ambedkar and Adam Smith. Amit adds his claim that Manmohan Singh did more for Dalits than any other twentieth-century thinker.
AlphaZero in chess: humans had to reverse-engineer its play to learn that initiative matters more than they had thought, just as humans must guess why credit algorithms flag certain behaviour.
China's government-run social credit score, which Amit calls 'creepy', contrasted with voluntary phone-data lending.
Sam Walton counting cars in Walmart parking lots to judge his business, the spark for satellite-based alternative data.
Alan Greenspan's view, per Ajay, that better measurement yields far bigger gains than more economic theory.
Hannah Arendt's line that authoritarians run out of people to oppress, invoked by Ajay in the fertility discussion.
Javier Milei, mentioned in the context of Argentina's inflation crisis. Amit says they'll do an episode on him once things settle.
